q: 1. Principle plane is a plane on which the shear stress is
explain: Principal planes are defined as planes where the shear stress component is zero.

q: 2. In Mohr's circle, the centre of circle from Y-axis is taken as
explain: The center of the Mohr's circle on the σ-axis is always the average of the two normal stresses: (σx + σy)/2.

q: 3. The extremities of any diameter on Mohr's circle represent
options: normal and shear stresses on a plane
explain: Any point on the circumference of a Mohr's circle represents the normal stress (σ) and shear stress (τ) on a specific plane.

q: 4. The energy stored in a body when strained within elastic limit is known as
explain: Strain energy is the internal work done by the force to deform a body, stored as potential energy while within the elastic limit.

q: 5. The total strain energy stored in a body is termed as
explain: Resilience is the total strain energy stored in a body within its elastic limit.

q: 6. Strain energy is the
options: energy stored in a body when strained within elastic limits
energy stored in a body when strained upto the breaking of a specimen
maximum strain energy which can be stored in a body
proof resilience per unit volume of a material
explain: As defined in Q. 327, it is the energy absorbed by a material when it is deformed elastically.

q: 7. The strain energy stored in a body, when suddenly loaded, is ............ the strain energy stored when same load is applied gradually.
explain: Sudden loading produces twice the stress of gradual loading. Since energy U = σ²V/2E, doubling the stress (2σ) results in 2² = 4 times the energy.

q: 8. Resilience is the
options: energy stored in a body when strained within elastic limits
energy stored in a body when strained upto the breaking of the specimen
maximum strain energy which can be stored in a body
explain: as per key d Resilience is the general capacity of a material to absorb energy when it is deformed elastically and release that energy upon unloading.

q: 9. The stress induced in a body, when suddenly loaded, is ............ the stress induced when the same load is applied gradually.
explain: For a suddenly applied load, the instantaneous stress reached is twice the value of the static stress produced by the same load.

q: 10. The strain energy stored in a spring, when subjected to maximum load, without suffering permanent distortion, is known as
explain: Proof resilience is the maximum strain energy a body can store without undergoing permanent (plastic) deformation.

q: 11. The capacity of a strained body for doing work on the removal of the straining force, is called
explain: This is another definition of resilience, emphasizing the ability to return to the original state and release stored energy.

q: 12. The maximum shear stress from a Mohr's circle is given by
options: the distance of centre from the origin
the distance of farthest point on the Mohr's circle from origin
explain: In Mohr's circle, the radius (R) directly represents the maximum shear stress value (τ_max).

q: 13. An element is subjected to two equal and like stress σ, on two mutually perpendicular planes. The shape of the Mohr's circle will be
explain: When σx = σy and τxy = 0, the radius R = √[((σx-σy)/2)² + τxy²] = 0. A circle with zero radius is a point located at (σ, 0).

q: 14. If the strains in the three principal directions are εx, εy and εz, the volumetric strain will be
explain: Volumetric strain (e_v) is the sum of the linear strains in three mutually perpendicular directions.

q: 15. The residual stress in a member is
options: the stress due to the loading on the member
the average of initial and final stresses
instantaneous stress due to sudden loading
explain: Based on the provided answer key (b), it refers to the average state of stress remaining after a cycle of loading/unloading.

q: 16. The stress along the contact surface of a rivet and the member is
explain: Bearing stress is the contact pressure that developed between two bodies (like a rivet and a plate) pushing against each other.

q: 17. In a stressed body the maximum normal stress at any point is always
options: average of maximum and minimum shear stresses
sum of the two normal stresses acting in two principal directions
explain: The maximum and minimum normal stresses acting on an element are the principal stresses.

q: 18. In a stressed body the minimum normal stress at any point is always
options: average of two normal stresses acting in the two principal directions
difference of two normal stresses in the two principal directions plus shear stresses on those planes
explain: As noted in Q. 340, both the maximum and minimum normal stresses are referred to as principal stresses.

q: 19. The maximum shear stress will be equal to
options: one half of the algebraic difference of the maximum and minimum principal stresses at the point
the intensity of shear stress acting on the major principal plane
the shear stress acting on the planes in the direction of two principal directions
explain: τ_max = (σ1 - σ2) / 2, where σ1 and σ2 are the major and minor principal stresses.

q: 20. The ratio of strengths of a rivet in double shear to that in a single shear will be
explain: In double shear, there are two planes resisting the shear force, effectively doubling the strength compared to a single shear plane.

q: 21. An isotropic material is the one which
options: has same structure at all the points
has Young's modulus equal to modulus of rigidity
has the elastic constants, identical in all the directions
explain: As established in Q. 277, isotropic materials exhibit the same elastic properties regardless of the direction of measurement.

q: 22. Twisting moment is a moment applied in the plane of cross-section acting about ............
explain: A twisting moment (torque) acts in the plane of the cross-section and causes rotation about the longitudinal axis of the member.

q: 23. When a member is subjected to a twisting moment, the material will be subjected to ............
explain: Torsion creates internal resistance in the form of shear stresses that act on the cross-sectional planes and longitudinal planes.

q: 24. If a shaft is subjected to pure twisting moment, an element on the surface is subjected to ............
explain: Under pure torsion, any element on the surface is in a state of pure shear, with no initial normal stresses acting on the plane of the cross-section.

q: 25. When a member is subjected to twisting moment the stress in any elemental ring will be proportional to ............
options: Modulus of rigidity of the material
explain: According to the torsion formula $\frac{\tau}{r} = \frac{T}{J}$, shear stress ($\tau$) is directly proportional to the radial distance ($r$) from the center.

q: 26. In a shaft subjected to pure torsion, maximum shear stress will occur at ............
options: a distance of semi-radius from centre
explain: Since shear stress is proportional to the radius ($r$), it is zero at the center and reaches its maximum value at the outer boundary (periphery) where $r=R$.

q: 27. What are the units of torque?
explain: Torque is defined as Force $\times$ perpendicular distance, hence its SI unit is Newton-meter (Nm).

q: 28. The torsional formula is valid if the shearing stresses ............
options: are within the shearing proportional limit
are caused due to twisting moment applied only at the free end
explain: The torsion formula assumes linear elastic behavior, meaning the shear stress must be within the proportional limit of the material.

q: 29. The diamond quadrilateral pyramid indenter is used in ............
explain: The Vickers hardness test uses a square-based diamond pyramid indenter with an angle of 136° between opposite faces.

q: 30. In Brinell Hardness test, the type of indenter used is ............
explain: The Brinell test uses a hardened steel (or tungsten carbide) ball of a specified diameter (usually 10mm) as the indenter.

q: 31. Glass will obey Hooke's law upto ............
explain: Glass is a perfectly brittle material. It shows almost no plastic deformation and fails (fractures) suddenly while still in the linear elastic range.

q: 32. The effect of the size of the specimen on ultimate strength will be more serious for ............
explain: Brittle materials are sensitive to flaws and surface defects, the probability of which increases with the volume/size of the specimen (Size Effect).

q: 33. The proportional limit of mild steel specimen is taken as the stress corresponding to a permanent set of ............
explain: While proof stress is often 0.2%, the limit of proportionality is very sensitive and is often associated with a very small permanent set like 0.01%.

q: 34. For structural carbon steel the ratio of yield stress to ultimate strength will be about ............
explain: For mild steel, the yield stress is typically around 60% (0.6) of the ultimate tensile strength.

q: 35. Within the elastic range of a tensile test the deviation from Hooke's law and some after effects may be noticed. This is due to ............
options: material does not at all obey Hooke's law
elastic limit is greater than ultimate strength
explain: Thermo-elastic effects involve small temperature changes during loading/unloading that can cause slight non-linearity even within the elastic range.

q: 36. Who introduced the terms upper and lower yield points?
explain: C. Bach is historically credited with the detailed investigation and nomenclature of the distinct yield points in mild steel.

q: 37. The lower yield point is more significant than upper yield point because ............
options: it is less than upper yield point
it is less influenced by shape of the specimen
it occurs before upper yield point
strain is more at this point
explain: The upper yield point is highly sensitive to the rate of loading and specimen alignment, whereas the lower yield point is a more stable material property.

q: 38. The compression test is commonly used for testing ............
explain: Brittle materials (like concrete, cast iron, or stone) are much stronger in compression than tension, making compression tests standard for them.

q: 39. When a cylindrical specimen of a ductile material is subjected to compression ............
options: it ultimately assumes the shape of a flat disc
it fails by fracture like a brittle material
it fails immediately after starting of loading
explain: Ductile materials under compression undergo significant plastic deformation (bulging) without fracturing, eventually flattening into a disc shape.

q: 40. What is strain energy?
options: the energy stored in a body because of being strained
the energy that is spent for straining a body
explain: Strain energy is the internal work done by external forces while deforming a body, which is stored as potential energy.

q: 41. The strain energy stored in a body due to an axial stress is ............
explain: The formula for strain energy ($U$) under axial load is $U = \frac{\sigma^2}{2E} \times V$.

q: 42. Strain energy due to bending stress is ............
explain: For a beam subjected to a bending moment $M$, the total strain energy is obtained by integrating $\frac{M^2}{2EI}$ over the length of the beam.

q: 43. What is the core of a section ............
options: portion where a compressive force applied causes no tension anywhere
the central portion of the cross-section of similar shape but half the area
area where compressive force will not cause any compressive stress
explain: The 'core' or 'kern' is the area within which an eccentric load can be applied without inducing any tensile stress in the section.

q: 44. To avoid any possibility of tension occurring in masonry structures, the resultant of various forces at any level must pass through ............
options: middle third of the width or depth of the section
explain: For rectangular sections (like masonry walls), the 'middle-third rule' states that the resultant must stay within the middle third to prevent tension.

q: 45. In the case of long columns the maximum permissible stress depends on ............
options: the ultimate crushing strength of the material
explain: Long columns fail by buckling. The critical stress is a function of the slenderness ratio (Le/r). As the slenderness ratio increases, the permissible buckling stress decreases.

q: 46. When a closed coiled helical spring is subjected to an axial tensile load the material of the spring will be subjected to ............
explain: An axial load on a closed coiled helical spring primarily induces a twisting moment (torsion) in the wire, resulting in torsional shear stress.

q: 47. When a close coiled helical spring is subjected to an axial twist, the material of the spring will be subjected to ............
explain: Applying an axial twist (torque) to the spring axis causes the wire itself to bend, thus inducing bending stresses in the material.

q: 48. If a shaft subjected to pure torsion cracks, the crack will start ............
explain: In torsion, the shear stress is maximum at the outer surface (periphery) and zero at the center. Therefore, failure/cracking initiates where the stress is highest.

q: 49. The ratio of the moment of inertia of a circular plate and that of a square plate for equal depth, is ............
explain: For depth (dimension) 'd': I(circle) = πd⁴/64, I(square) = d⁴/12. Ratio = (πd⁴/64) / (d⁴/12) = 12π/64 = 3π/16.

q: 50. The intensity of direct longitudinal stress in the cross-section at any point distant r from the neutral axis, is proportional to ............
explain: According to the bending equation (M/I = σ/y), the bending stress (σ) is directly proportional to the distance (y or r) from the neutral axis.
